pages.page_context:
# Basic Sharpening

Sharpening removes steel until the two sides of the cutting edge meet again in a clean apex. A beginner does not need speed, a large collection of stones or perfect knowledge of metallurgy. The essential skills are simpler:

- place the narrow **edge bevel** on the stone;
- keep the same local contact angle along the complete edge;
- let both the forward and return movement sharpen;
- work the two sides evenly;
- listen to how the contact changes;
- create and then remove a small continuous burr.

This method is intended for ordinary double-bevel kitchen knives. Traditional single-bevel knives need a different method and should be learned separately.

## 1. Inspect the knife

Look along the cutting edge under strong light. Dull, rolled or chipped areas often reflect light. Check the tip, curved front, middle and heel.

A normally dull knife can usually be sharpened on one medium stone. A chipped edge, a broken tip or a knife that has become very thick behind the edge needs repair or geometry work. Those operations remove much more steel and are outside this beginner method.

## 2. Find the edge bevel

A kitchen knife has several different surfaces near the edge. The broad primary bevel makes the blade thinner toward the cutting edge. The **edge bevel** is the much narrower facet immediately beside the apex. When this facet is especially narrow and deliberately distinct from the geometry behind it, it is often called a **microbevel**.

Routine sharpening of an ordinary double-bevel knife usually works on this narrow edge bevel. Laying the whole broad primary bevel on the stone changes the blade geometry and removes much more steel than necessary.

A marker is the easiest learning aid. Colour only the narrow edge bevel and make a few light movements on the stone. Then inspect the ink:

- ink left at the apex means the angle is too low;
- contact only on the extreme edge means the angle is steeper than the existing edge bevel;
- ink removed evenly across the narrow facet means the contact is close to correct.

As a rough visual reference, raise the spine until the gap between the spine and the stone is about one quarter of the blade's height. This corresponds to roughly 15 degrees per side on a simple flat approximation. It is only a starting reference: following the existing edge bevel is more useful than forcing every knife to one number.

## 3. Position the hands

Hold the handle firmly but without tension. The handle hand controls the knife's direction and contact angle. Rest the fingers of the other hand on the blade face, safely above the edge, near the section that is crossing the stone.

Keep the shoulders relaxed and use the arms and upper body for the movement. A rigid wrist and excessive grip make the angle harder to control.

In the method taught in this book, when you turn the knife to sharpen the second side, also change the hand that holds the handle. This gives the second face a movement that mirrors the first and can make it easier for a beginner to preserve the same contact angle. Other experienced sharpeners may use different hand arrangements successfully; the important result is stable, controlled contact with the existing edge bevel.

Practise the movement slowly with almost no pressure until both hands can follow the full edge comfortably.

## 4. Use the complete stone and complete edge

Set the knife diagonally on the stone. Begin with the tip area in contact, then sweep the blade sideways so the working point travels through the curved front and middle to the heel. Reverse the movement and return along the same path.

Both the outward movement and the return movement can sharpen the knife when angle and pressure remain controlled. In this method, the return is used as an active sharpening stroke rather than only as a reset. This back-and-forth action makes the work faster and practical for a beginner.

Move the supporting fingers with the section being sharpened. Do not leave all the pressure in the middle of the blade. Use the full surface of the stone so that the stone and knife both wear more evenly.

## 5. Follow the changing blade profile

The cutting edge is rarely straight from heel to tip. Its curve changes the way each section meets the flat stone.

Adapt the grip and orientation of the knife continuously so that the **contact angle between the stone and the local edge bevel remains the same along the whole cutting edge**, despite changes in the blade's shape. Watch and feel the contact from tip through the curved section, middle and heel.

Think about preserving contact, not performing a separate gesture at the tip. There is no instruction to lift the handle by a predetermined amount. Each knife has a different profile, so the hands must follow the actual blade in front of them.

Use the marker again if the tip or heel remains untouched. It shows whether the movement follows the full edge bevel without making the front of the edge unnecessarily steep.

## 6. Listen to the stone

Sound is one of the most useful guides during sharpening.

At the beginning, contact often produces a strong scratching noise. The blade may also feel rough against the stone. Continue with a stable angle and controlled pressure. As the stone evens the edge bevel, the sound normally becomes smoother and the blade begins to glide more freely. A good, even contact can resemble the smooth sound of skis moving over snow.

Listen to the complete journey from tip to heel. A sudden harsh sound or change in resistance at one point may show that the angle changed, the stone is becoming dry or that one section needs more work.

Do not count a fixed number of passes. The required work changes with the knife, steel, stone and pressure. Instead, listen for the sound to move from scratching toward smooth sliding. When it no longer changes over several complete movements, the stone has usually worked the edge bevel evenly. Confirm this with the marker pattern and visual inspection.

Sound is feedback, not proof by itself. The burr confirms that the abrasive has reached the apex.

## 7. Progress evenly on both sides

During the first stage, change sides from time to time. In the method taught here, also change the handle hand. Give the two faces a broadly similar amount of work so that the edge develops evenly. The aim is balance, not an exact numerical count.

Check occasionally for a burr. If one forms almost immediately, inspect the angle before doing more work: an angle that is too steep can create a burr quickly at the cost of a wider and less efficient edge.

When the sound has become stable and the marker shows even contact, work one side until the smallest detectable burr runs continuously from heel to tip. Then change side and work the other face until the burr moves back along the complete edge.

If the burr is missing only in one area, concentrate briefly on that area and then return to complete passes. Avoid continuing heavy work on sections that have already reached the apex.

## 8. Reduce pressure and remove the burr

The main sharpening stage creates the new apex. The finishing stage cleans and stabilizes it.

Reduce pressure gradually. Alternate sides more frequently. If you are following the hand-switching method taught here, change the handle hand each time. Continue using the full outward and return movement, but let the blade become progressively lighter on the stone.

Finish with only enough pressure to keep the edge bevel in contact. Check that no rough directional hook remains on either side. A large or persistent burr usually responds better to lighter, more controlled passes than to further heavy grinding.

A strop can remove a very fine remaining burr, but it is optional. The stone should already have produced a clean and stable edge.

## 9. Decide whether a finer stone is useful

A medium finish is practical for most kitchen work and keeps useful bite on tomato skin, meat and fibrous vegetables. A finer stone can produce a smoother edge for delicate slicing or push cutting.

Move to a finer stone only after the first stone has reached the apex along the whole edge and the burr is under control. Use the same contact method with less pressure. A higher grit is a finishing choice, not proof of better sharpening.

## 10. Test the result

Rinse and dry the knife before testing it.

Do not use your fingers to test whether the knife is sharp. Finger contact at the edge is used only to detect a burr during sharpening, with the controlled perpendicular method described in [The Burr](the-burr.md). Test sharpness only by cutting suitable food or paper.

### Look at the edge

Inspect the apex under strong light. A clean sharp edge reflects very little. Bright points can reveal a remaining flat, roll or small chip.

### Check the burr

Check heel, middle, curved front and tip. Neither side should have a directional hook.

### Cut paper slowly

Hold a clean dry sheet with the supporting hand far from the cutting path. Start near the heel and draw the edge smoothly through the paper toward the tip. Do not make a fast, uncontrolled slash.

Notice where resistance changes. A catch or tear identifies an area that needs attention. On a long knife, test heel to middle and then middle to tip in two overlapping sections.

### Test on suitable food

A tomato shows whether the edge enters a resistant skin without pressure. An onion shows whether it passes cleanly through layers. Herbs reveal crushing. Choose a test that matches the knife's intended work.

Paper can be cut by a fragile wire edge, so combine the paper test with the burr check and real cutting behaviour.

## Practical advice that improves the result

### Use the abrasive instead of extra pressure

More pressure is rarely the answer to slow progress. Heavy pressure makes the angle unstable and creates a larger burr. If the stone hardly removes steel, it may be too fine, glazed or unsuitable for that steel.

### Keep the stone wet and stable

A dry or moving stone changes both sound and control. Add water when the surface drags and stop immediately if the support moves.

### Correct only the area that needs more work

If the tip, middle or heel has received less sharpening, give that area a short period of focused work. Then return to complete passes so the finished edge remains connected and even.

### Keep the burr small

The burr is evidence that the apex has been reached. It is not something to enlarge. Stop the heavy stage as soon as it is light and continuous.

### Accept slow, controlled movements

Speed does not improve the edge. A slow movement that maintains edge-bevel contact teaches more than a rapid movement with an unstable angle.

## Common beginner mistakes

- sharpening the broad primary bevel instead of the narrow edge bevel;
- fixing the hands in one position while the blade profile changes;
- wasting the return stroke when using the back-and-forth method taught here;
- changing side without first establishing a comfortable, controlled hand position;
- counting passes instead of listening and inspecting;
- treating an immediate burr as proof that the angle is correct;
- overworking the middle while missing the tip or heel;
- using heavy pressure during finishing;
- leaving the burr attached;
- moving to a fine stone before the first stone has reached the apex.

## Basic-level self-test

You are ready to practise more independently when you can answer **yes** to all of these questions:

1. Can you identify the edge bevel and confirm its contact with a marker?
2. Can you use both directions of the movement without losing the local angle?
3. Can you follow the entire edge while keeping continuous edge-bevel contact?
4. Can you change side and establish a stable hand position comfortably?
5. Can you hear the change from rough scratching to smoother sliding?
6. Can you keep the work broadly balanced without relying on a fixed pass count?
7. Can you detect a light burr safely at heel, middle, curve and tip?
8. Can you move the burr to the other side and then remove it with lighter alternating passes?
9. Can the finished edge cut consistently along its whole length without a remaining directional hook?

If one answer is no, repeat that specific part on an inexpensive practice knife. The purpose of the basic level is not speed or polish. It is complete, controlled and repeatable contact with the edge bevel.

## The complete routine in brief

1. Prepare a flat, wet and stable medium stone.
2. Inspect the edge and mark the edge bevel.
3. Set the local contact angle.
4. Sharpen in both directions across the complete edge using the controlled back-and-forth method taught here.
5. Adapt the grip continuously to preserve the same contact angle through every change in blade profile.
6. Listen as the sound changes from scratching to smooth sliding.
7. Alternate sides periodically, keeping the work broadly equal; if following this book's method, switch the handle hand as well.
8. Confirm a small continuous burr on one side, then move it from the other.
9. Reduce pressure, alternate sides and remove the burr.
10. Inspect, test, clean and dry the knife and stone.

The most important skill is learning to interpret the contact between the knife and the stone. The marker shows where the stone touches, the sound shows how that contact is changing and the burr confirms that the work has reached the apex.

units.masked_source: Sound is one of the most useful guides during sharpening.

units.source: At the beginning, contact often produces a strong scratching noise. The blade may also feel rough against the stone. Continue with a stable angle and controlled pressure. As the stone evens the edge bevel, the sound normally becomes smoother and the blade begins to glide more freely. A good, even contact can resemble the smooth sound of skis moving over snow.

units.source: Listen to the complete journey from tip to heel. A sudden harsh sound or change in resistance at one point may show that the angle changed, the stone is becoming dry or that one section needs more work.
units.masked_source: Listen to the complete journey from tip to heel. A sudden harsh sound or change in resistance at one point may show that the angle changed, the stone is becoming dry or that one section needs more work.

units.source: Do not count a fixed number of passes. The required work changes with the knife, steel, stone and pressure. Instead, listen for the sound to move from scratching toward smooth sliding. units.source: ## 7. Progress evenly on both sides

units.source: During the first stage, change sides from time to time. In the method taught here, also change the handle hand. Give the two faces a broadly similar amount of work so that the edge develops evenly. The aim is balance, not an exact numerical count.

units.source: Check occasionally for a burr. If one forms almost immediately, inspect the angle before doing more work: an angle that is too steep can create a burr quickly at the cost of a wider and less efficient edge.

units.source: The main sharpening stage creates the new apex. The finishing stage cleans and stabilizes it.

units.source: Reduce pressure gradually. Alternate sides more frequently. If you are following the hand-switching method taught here, change the handle hand each time. Continue using the full outward and return movement, but let the blade become progressively lighter on the stone.

units.source: ## 9. Decide whether a finer stone is useful

units.source: ## 10. Test the result

units.source: ### Cut paper slowly

units.masked_source: ## Practical advice that improves the result

units.source: ### Use the abrasive instead of extra pressure
units.masked_source: ### Use the abrasive instead of extra pressure

units.source: ### Correct only the area that needs more work

units.source: ## The complete routine in brief
units.masked_source: ## The complete routine in brief

units.source:
1. Prepare a flat, wet and stable medium stone.
2. Inspect the edge and mark the edge bevel.
3. Set the local contact angle.
4. Sharpen in both directions across the complete edge using the controlled back-and-forth method taught here.
5. Adapt the grip continuously to preserve the same contact angle through every change in blade profile.
6. Listen as the sound changes from scratching to smooth sliding.
7. Alternate sides periodically, keeping the work broadly equal; if following this book's method, switch the handle hand as well.
8. Confirm a small continuous burr on one side, then move it from the other.
9. Reduce pressure, alternate sides and remove the burr.
10. Inspect, test, clean and dry the knife and stone.

# The Burr

The previous chapter already used the burr as part of the **basic sharpening process**. This chapter does not add a new stage that happens after sharpening. It pauses to explain that same feedback signal in more detail: what the burr is, what it proves, how to detect it safely and why removing it is as important as creating it.

The burr is the beginner's clearest proof that the stone has reached the cutting edge.

As one side is sharpened, the steel at the apex becomes extremely thin. The abrasive eventually bends a tiny lip of metal toward the opposite side. This lip is the **burr**.

The goal is a very small burr that can be detected along the whole edge. A large burr wastes steel and is harder to remove. It can also behave like a fragile wire: the knife seems sharp at first, then loses its edge when the wire folds or breaks.

## How to check it safely

Never slide a finger along the cutting edge.

This is not a sharpness test. In this guide, the only reason to bring a fingertip to the edge is to detect a burr during sharpening. Test the knife's sharpness only by cutting suitable food or paper.

Hold the knife still and use very light pressure. Move the pad of a finger from the blade face toward the edge, perpendicular to it, and stop at the apex. Check the heel, middle, curved front and tip. The burr feels like a slight rough hook on the side opposite the one just sharpened.

If you prefer not to touch near the edge, use a cotton pad or soft cloth fibre. It may catch on the burr. Good light and magnification can also reveal parts of the edge that still reflect light.

Clean the blade before checking. Slurry and loose steel particles can otherwise feel like a burr.

## What the burr indicates

A burr at only one point proves that the stone reached the apex only there. A light continuous burr from heel to tip confirms that the whole side has reached the edge.

Check it occasionally while working, especially while learning. A burr can appear almost immediately when the angle is too steep. In that case, the stone may be touching only the extreme edge and creating a new, steeper edge bevel. A quick burr therefore proves contact with the apex, but it does not by itself prove that the angle is correct. Check the marker pattern and the width of the edge bevel before continuing.

When the angle is correct, stop the main work on that side as soon as the smallest detectable burr is continuous. More heavy passes only enlarge it.

## Moving and removing the burr

After the first side reaches the apex, sharpen the second side with the same path and local contact angle. If you are following the hand-switching method taught in this book, change the hand holding the knife when you change sides. The burr should move back toward the first side along the whole edge.

Then reduce pressure and alternate sides. The last passes should be much lighter than the working passes. Their purpose is to centre the apex and weaken the burr rather than remove substantial steel.

There is no useful fixed count. The steel, stone, pressure and initial condition of the knife all change the amount of work required. Continue until neither face has a directional hook and the edge feels consistent from heel to tip.

A leather or fabric strop can help remove a very fine remaining burr. Move the knife spine-first and use little pressure so the edge does not cut into the strop or become rounded. Stropping is helpful but optional; careful light work on the stone is the essential step.

## The practical rule

Use the burr as a check during sharpening, not as the final goal:

1. reach the apex with the smallest continuous burr;
2. repeat on the other side until the burr changes direction;
3. reduce pressure and alternate sides;
4. finish only when the weakened metal has been removed.

A knife that still has a wire edge may cut paper once and fail in food. A clean, stable apex should keep cutting after the test.

pages.page_context:
# Sharpening Setup

Good sharpening begins with a stable, flat and correctly wetted stone. Careful preparation makes the movement easier to control and prevents many mistakes that beginners wrongly blame on their technique.

This chapter prepares the stone and workstation only. The next chapter uses that setup to teach the complete basic sharpening sequence.

## A simple first setup

For an ordinary kitchen knife that has become dull through normal use, one good medium-grit water stone is usually enough. A stone around 800-1500 grit can rebuild a practical kitchen edge without adding unnecessary steps.

A coarse stone is useful for chips, a very rounded edge or a deliberate change of geometry. A finer stone can make the finished edge smoother, but it is optional. A fine stone cannot compensate for an edge that was never properly sharpened on the first stone.

You also need:

- a non-slip stone holder or a damp cloth;
- water or the lubricant required by the stone manufacturer;
- a clean cloth;
- good light;
- enough clear space to move the complete blade over the stone.

## Prepare the stone correctly

Water stones do not all work in the same way. Some absorb water and need to soak. Others need only water on the surface and are often called **splash-and-go** stones. Diamond plates do not soak, and oil stones use oil rather than water.

Follow the manufacturer's instructions whenever they are available. For a traditional absorbent water stone, soak it until the stream of air bubbles has almost stopped. Do not leave an unknown stone submerged for hours: long soaking can damage some binders.

Keep the working surface wet during sharpening. Add water when the blade begins to drag, the sound becomes dry or dark residue stops moving freely. The grey mixture on the stone contains water, abrasive and removed steel. It is not the burr, which remains attached to the cutting edge.

## Check that the stone is flat

A stone wears most where the knife passes most often. With use, its centre can become hollow. A hollow surface changes the contact angle during the stroke and makes a consistent result much harder.

Place a straight edge across the stone in several directions and look for gaps. Pencil lines drawn across the surface are another useful check: during flattening, high areas lose the marks first and low areas keep them.

Flatten the stone with a suitable plate or lapping stone when necessary. A beginner does not need microscopic perfection, but the surface should form one reliable plane.

## Make the workspace stable

Place the stone on a holder, rubber base or folded damp cloth. Push it gently before beginning. It should not slide or rock.

Stand or sit at a height that lets you relax your shoulders and move your arms freely. Leave space for the knife to travel across the stone from tip to heel. Keep the area free from objects that could stop the movement.

The hand holding the handle controls direction and angle. The other hand rests lightly on the blade and applies pressure near the part of the edge that is crossing the stone. Keep the fingers above the blade face and away from the cutting edge.

## After sharpening

Rinse the knife and dry it immediately. Rinse the stone, remove loose residue and check whether it needs light flattening.

Let a water stone dry slowly in a ventilated place. Avoid radiators, ovens, strong sunlight and closed containers while the stone is still damp. Store it only when it is completely dry.

The preparation target is simple: a stone that is suitable for the work, correctly wetted, reasonably flat and completely stable. Once those conditions are set, move to [Basic Sharpening](basic-sharpening-process.md) and concentrate on contact, angle, pressure and feedback rather than on the equipment.

units.masked_source: For an ordinary kitchen knife that has become dull through normal use, one good medium-grit water stone is usually enough. A stone around 800-1500 grit can rebuild a practical kitchen edge without adding unnecessary steps.

units.source: A coarse stone is useful for chips, a very rounded edge or a deliberate change of geometry. A finer stone can make the finished edge smoother, but it is optional. A fine stone cannot compensate for an edge that was never properly sharpened on the first stone.
units.masked_source: A coarse stone is useful for chips, a very rounded edge or a deliberate change of geometry. A finer stone can make the finished edge smoother, but it is optional. A fine stone cannot compensate for an edge that was never properly sharpened on the first stone.

units.masked_source: You also need:

units.source: ## Prepare the stone correctly
units.masked_source: ## Prepare the stone correctly

units.source: Water stones do not all work in the same way. Some absorb water and need to soak. Others need only water on the surface and are often called **splash-and-go** stones. Diamond plates do not soak, and oil stones use oil rather than water.
units.masked_source: Water stones do not all work in the same way. Some absorb water and need to soak. Others need only water on the surface and are often called **splash-and-go** stones. Diamond plates do not soak, and oil stones use oil rather than water.

units.source: Follow the manufacturer's instructions whenever they are available. For a traditional absorbent water stone, soak it until the stream of air bubbles has almost stopped. Do not leave an unknown stone submerged for hours: long soaking can damage some binders.
units.masked_source: Follow the manufacturer's instructions whenever they are available. For a traditional absorbent water stone, soak it until the stream of air bubbles has almost stopped. Do not leave an unknown stone submerged for hours: long soaking can damage some binders.

units.source: Keep the working surface wet during sharpening. Add water when the blade begins to drag, the sound becomes dry or dark residue stops moving freely. The grey mixture on the stone contains water, abrasive and removed steel. It is not the burr, which remains attached to the cutting edge.
units.masked_source: Keep the working surface wet during sharpening. Add water when the blade begins to drag, the sound becomes dry or dark residue stops moving freely. The grey mixture on the stone contains water, abrasive and removed steel. It is not the burr, which remains attached to the cutting edge.

units.source: ## Check that the stone is flat
units.masked_source: ## Check that the stone is flat

units.source: A stone wears most where the knife passes most often. With use, its centre can become hollow. A hollow surface changes the contact angle during the stroke and makes a consistent result much harder.
units.masked_source: A stone wears most where the knife passes most often. With use, its centre can become hollow. A hollow surface changes the contact angle during the stroke and makes a consistent result much harder.

units.source: Place a straight edge across the stone in several directions and look for gaps. Pencil lines drawn across the surface are another useful check: during flattening, high areas lose the marks first and low areas keep them.
units.masked_source: Place a straight edge across the stone in several directions and look for gaps. Pencil lines drawn across the surface are another useful check: during flattening, high areas lose the marks first and low areas keep them.

units.source: Flatten the stone with a suitable plate or lapping stone when necessary. A beginner does not need microscopic perfection, but the surface should form one reliable plane.
units.masked_source: Flatten the stone with a suitable plate or lapping stone when necessary. A beginner does not need microscopic perfection, but the surface should form one reliable plane.

units.source: ## Make the workspace stable
units.masked_source: ## Make the workspace stable

units.source: Place the stone on a holder, rubber base or folded damp cloth. Push it gently before beginning. It should not slide or rock.
units.masked_source: Place the stone on a holder, rubber base or folded damp cloth. Push it gently before beginning. It should not slide or rock.

units.source: Stand or sit at a height that lets you relax your shoulders and move your arms freely. Leave space for the knife to travel across the stone from tip to heel. Keep the area free from objects that could stop the movement.
units.masked_source: Stand or sit at a height that lets you relax your shoulders and move your arms freely. Leave space for the knife to travel across the stone from tip to heel. Keep the area free from objects that could stop the movement.

units.source: The hand holding the handle controls direction and angle. The other hand rests lightly on the blade and applies pressure near the part of the edge that is crossing the stone. Keep the fingers above the blade face and away from the cutting edge.
units.masked_source: The hand holding the handle controls direction and angle. The other hand rests lightly on the blade and applies pressure near the part of the edge that is crossing the stone. Keep the fingers above the blade face and away from the cutting edge.

units.source: ## After sharpening
units.masked_source: ## After sharpening

units.source: Rinse the knife and dry it immediately. Rinse the stone, remove loose residue and check whether it needs light flattening.
units.masked_source: Rinse the knife and dry it immediately. Rinse the stone, remove loose residue and check whether it needs light flattening.

units.source: Let a water stone dry slowly in a ventilated place. Avoid radiators, ovens, strong sunlight and closed containers while the stone is still damp. Store it only when it is completely dry.
units.masked_source: Let a water stone dry slowly in a ventilated place. Avoid radiators, ovens, strong sunlight and closed containers while the stone is still damp. Store it only when it is completely dry.

units.source: The preparation target is simple: a stone that is suitable for the work, correctly wetted, reasonably flat and completely stable. Once those conditions are set, move to [Basic Sharpening](basic-sharpening-process.md) and concentrate on contact, angle, pressure and feedback rather than on the equipment.
units.masked_source: The preparation target is simple: a stone that is suitable for the work, correctly wetted, reasonably flat and completely stable. Once those conditions are set, move to [Basic Sharpening](⟦KBT0001⟧) and concentrate on contact, angle, pressure and feedback rather than on the equipment.

pages.page_context:
# Bibliography

All bibliographic, technical and historical sources cited throughout the book are collected here so that the individual chapters remain focused on the explanation itself. Entries are grouped by the chapter in which they are used.

<!-- bibliography-source: 01-foundations/five-dimensions-of-knife-steel.md -->
## The Five Dimensions of Knife Steel

- [Rockwell and Rockwell, US Patent 1,294,171, Hardness Tester](https://patents.google.com/patent/US1294171A/en)
- [worldstainless, Stainless Steel Terminology](https://worldstainless.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/terminology.pdf)
- [British Stainless Steel Association, When is stainless steel passive or active?](https://bssa.org.uk/bssa_articles/when-is-stainless-steel-passive-or-active-formation-of-the-passive-layer/)
- [British Stainless Steel Association, The Discovery of Stainless Steel](https://bssa.org.uk/bssa_articles/the-discovery-of-stainless-steel/)
- [Knife Steel Nerds, Carbide Types in Knife Steels](https://knifesteelnerds.com/2019/07/15/carbide-types-in-knife-steels/)
- [Knife Steel Nerds, Which Steel Has the Best Edge Retention? Part 2](https://knifesteelnerds.com/2018/11/26/steel-edge-retention2/)
- [Knife Steel Nerds, Which Knife Steels Have the Best Corrosion Resistance?](https://knifesteelnerds.com/2019/01/14/which-knife-steels-have-the-best-corrosion-resistance/)
<!-- /bibliography-source -->

<!-- bibliography-source: 02-steels-and-metallurgy/alloying-elements.md -->
## Alloying Elements

- [worldstainless, Stainless Steel Terminology](https://worldstainless.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/terminology.pdf)
- [British Stainless Steel Association, When is stainless steel passive or active?](https://bssa.org.uk/bssa_articles/when-is-stainless-steel-passive-or-active-formation-of-the-passive-layer/)
- [Knife Steel Nerds, Which Knife Steels Have the Best Corrosion Resistance?](https://knifesteelnerds.com/2019/01/14/which-knife-steels-have-the-best-corrosion-resistance/)
- [Knife Steel Nerds, Carbon vs Stainless Steel in Knives](https://knifesteelnerds.com/2018/09/10/carbon-vs-stainless-steel-in-knives/)
- [William Lox, "Bintie: The Wootz Steel in Ancient China," *Indian Journal of History of Science* 44.3 (2009)](https://insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/IJHS/Vol44_3_2_WLox.pdf)
<!-- /bibliography-source -->

<!-- bibliography-source: 02-steels-and-metallurgy/conventional-and-powder-metallurgy-steels.md -->
## Conventional and Powder-Metallurgy Steels

- [The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, *Professional Guide on Steel*, section 2.2.2: Iron-carbon phase diagram](https://www.polyu.edu.hk/cnercsteel/-/media/department/cnercsteel/publication/professional-guide/eqsteel_20211115.pdf)

pages.page_context:
# Preface

The title of this book comes from an idea much broader than martial arts. *Gongfu* can describe a skill built through time, study, repetition and disciplined practice: knowledge turned into reliable ability.

That is the spirit of this book. A kitchen knife looks simple, but using one well takes more than learning a few movements. Skill grows faster when practice is supported by understanding: when the user knows why a knife behaves as it does, can separate meaningful differences from superficial ones and can connect what is felt in the hand with the choices behind the tool.

This book provides a technical and practical foundation for developing that competence. It cannot replace years of professional experience, and reading alone cannot create mastery. Its purpose is to make practice more effective: to help the reader observe carefully, understand established solutions, ask better questions and learn faster from experience. *Gongfu* begins by learning what others have discovered, then practising until those principles can be understood, judged, adapted and eventually improved.

The book combines personal study and experience with knowledge drawn from Xinzuo's work in product development, manufacturing, testing and direct contact with professional and home users. This practical perspective allows general principles of knife design and use to be examined through real decisions about materials, processes, geometry and construction. The aim is not simply to describe Xinzuo knives, but to use them as concrete examples through which the reader can develop the judgement needed to choose, use and care for a kitchen knife well.

## Why I wrote this book

This project began inside Xinzuo from a practical company need: **to train the people who work with our knives**. Knowledge about steels, heat treatment, blade geometry, construction, sharpening, use and maintenance existed across different people and different parts of the company, but it was not always collected in one place. A colleague learning how to explain, recommend or support a product should have access to the same dependable technical foundation regardless of who happens to be available to teach them that day.

The first purpose of the book is therefore still the one that gave birth to it. **It is intended to be a principal training guide for Xinzuo staff and for people who need to understand these products professionally.** It should provide a shared language and a practical body of knowledge that can support product training, demonstrations, customer advice and day-to-day work.

As the material grew, however, another point became increasingly clear: the questions asked by a new member of staff are often the same questions asked by cooks, enthusiasts, students, customers and people who are simply curious about knives. Why does one steel behave differently from another? What does forging really mean? Why does balance change with the grip? Why are two apparently similar knives designed differently? These are not questions that belong only to people who work in the knife industry.

That realization did not replace the original training purpose; it added a second one. **This book is also intended to make the world of kitchen knives easier to understand for a much wider public, including readers with no professional connection to the sector.** It aims to share technical knowledge in a form that remains rigorous enough for training while being clear and useful to anyone who wants to understand the materials, manufacturing choices, geometry, sharpening, use and care behind a good kitchen knife.

The book therefore has two connected roles: **a working foundation for professional training and a public guide for learning and dissemination**. The same explanation should help a colleague advise a customer more accurately and help an interested reader make a more informed choice, use a knife more safely or simply understand a subject they find fascinating.

## Why this book is about Xinzuo

There is also a personal reason Xinzuo became the frame of reference for this book. In my professional work as EU Brand and Operations Manager at Xinzuo, what interested me was not a single model or specification, but the way product development connects materials, manufacturing processes and design. The book itself, however, is a personal project: I wrote it in my own capacity, drawing on that experience rather than as an official corporate publication.

That work extends far beyond designing a blade shape or choosing an attractive finish. Xinzuo works on steels, heat treatment, powder metallurgy, layered constructions, handle materials, balance, ergonomics, grinding, sharpening and testing. It uses established specialist steels when they are the right solution, but it also develops proprietary metallurgy such as 14Cr14MoVNb with industrial and academic partners. Selected series use demanding processes such as vacuum heat treatment and deep-freeze processing, while water-cooled grinding and whetstone sharpening protect the heat-treated edge during final manufacturing. Different steels, constructions, handle materials and balance strategies are used because different cooks, grips and tasks require different compromises.

That combination of manufacturing experience and continued experimentation shaped the way I learned to think about knives. Established solutions are respected, but materials, processes and designs are still examined against the question of whether they can be improved. Much of the knowledge collected in this book grew from working in that environment and from trying to make those decisions understandable to others.

Knowledge improves when it is shared. This book is also available free of charge on GitHub at **https://github.com/francescocmazza/xinzuo-kung-fu**. The repository supports collaborative revision, and corrections, comments and proposals are welcome there or by email at **francescoclaudiomazza@gmail.com**.

This book is a starting point: knowledge becomes practice, practice becomes experience, and experience can become *gongfu*.

**Francesco Claudio Mazza**

pages.translation_guidance: Write polished, natural Dutch editorial prose for readers interested in professional cooking, kitchen knives, sharpening and metallurgy. Prefer established Dutch technical terminology and avoid literal English syntax.
pages.page_context: # Anatomy of a Kitchen Knife Before comparing blade shapes, steels or sharpening angles, understand a knife as three connected systems: the cutting geometry, the steel structure that supports it and the hand interface that controls it. The names below locate each feature within those systems. Not every knife has every feature named in this chapter. The exploded image below shows a Western full-tang construction. Asian hidden-tang handles use a different construction, described later in this chapter. ## From edge to hand A fixed kitchen knife begins with the **blade**. Its front ends at the **tip**; the upper unsharpened side is the **spine**; the broad side is the **blade face**; the sharpened lower boundary is the **cutting edge**; and the rear of the cutting portion is the **heel**. The sloping geometry leading to the edge is the **bevel**. The visible texture or polish on the blade face is the **surface finish**. Behind the blade, the steel continues as the **tang**. On many Western knives the tang is visible around the handle and covered on both sides by **handle scales**, usually fixed with adhesive and **rivets or pins**. Many Western kitchen knives also have a metal **bolster** between blade and handle. The rear end of the handle is the **butt** or **pommel**. ## Blade terminology The **tip** is the front of the blade. Its shape affects how easily the knife enters small spaces, scores a surface or makes fine directional corrections. The **spine** is the upper, normally unsharpened side. Its thickness and taper toward the tip affect stiffness, balance and how easily the blade passes through food. The broad side is the **blade face**. It is not always flat: convexity, hollows, cladding transitions and other shaping can change how food moves against it. The **surface finish** is the final texture or appearance on that face, such as satin, polished, mirror-polished, brushed, etched or hammered. Finish and geometry are different: two blades can look similar while having very different thickness and cross-section. The **cutting edge** or **edge** is the sharpened line that enters the food. Above it, the **bevel** narrows the blade toward the apex. Some knives have a clearly visible primary bevel; on others the transition is subtle. The **heel** is the rear of the cutting edge, closest to the handle. Depending on the design, a short unsharpened area or relief may separate it from the bolster or handle. ## Handle, bolster and tang The **handle** is the part held by the user, but its construction varies. On a Western **full-tang** knife, the tang runs through almost the full length and outline of the handle. **Scales** cover its sides and are usually secured with adhesive and **rivets or pins**. The exposed steel can add mass and affect balance. **Full tang is only one valid tang construction.** A **hidden tang** is narrower than the handle and enclosed inside it. Some hidden tangs extend all the way to the butt and are mechanically secured there; this is a **through tang**, a separate construction term and not another name for a full tang. A **partial or stub tang** ends before the butt. Molded handles can encapsulate the tang so no scales or rivets are visible. These constructions should not be treated as a simple quality hierarchy: durability depends on tang dimensions, materials, fit, fastening, intended use and expected loads. With the tang identified, the next part to distinguish is the **blade-to-handle transition**. A **bolster** is the reinforced metal transition found on many Western kitchen knives. It may be integral with the blade or manufactured as a separate component. It can strengthen the transition, create a comfortable finger contact point, protect the front of the handle and add mass near the hand. Some bolsters extend to the heel; others leave the edge open for easier sharpening. A bolster is not necessarily a **guard**. A guard is specifically designed to stop the hand sliding toward the edge, and many kitchen knives have no separate guard. On many high-quality production knives, a separate bolster is joined to the blade-and-tang assembly by **welding** and is then ground and finished as part of the complete knife. The presence of a welded joint is not, by itself, a sign of lower quality. In hurried or poorly controlled manufacture, inaccurate fit or an inadequate joint can make this transition a structurally sensitive point. When the parts fit correctly and the joint, heat control and finishing are properly executed, the bolster can instead stiffen and reinforce the blade-to-handle transition and help distribute loads through that area. A common question is why the bolster is not simply made from the same high-performance steel as the blade. The first reason is functional: the bolster does not form the cutting edge, so using an expensive specialist blade steel there usually adds material cost without improving cutting performance. A separate component allows each material to be chosen for the work it actually performs: the blade steel for edge behaviour and the bolster material for structure, corrosion resistance, finish, manufacturability and reliable joining. There is also an important manufacturing reason. If an integral bolster is produced by **machining from uniform plate or bar stock**, the starting material has to be at least as thick as the bolster even though the blade and much of the tang are far thinner. A large proportion of that expensive steel must then be removed to create the final blade geometry. This wastes both premium material and machining time. Forging can create an integral bolster by a different route and reduces the need to machine the whole knife from bolster-thickness stock, so the exact economics depend on the manufacturing process. In production based on plate or bar, however, making the bolster separately is often the more rational solution: expensive blade steel is concentrated where its properties matter instead of being consumed simply to create a thick non-cutting section. ### What forging actually means That manufacturing comparison raises a term that is often mistaken for a quality label. **Forging is a manufacturing process, not a quality grade.** The steel remains solid and is reshaped by compressive force so that material moves from one part of the workpiece to another. Knife forging is usually done hot because heated steel requires less force to deform. A hand hammer is only one way to supply that force: power hammers, mechanical or hydraulic presses and industrial dies can all forge steel. A knife can therefore be genuinely forged without being handmade, and a hand-forged knife is not automatically a better knife. The practical contrast is with **stock removal**. In stock-removal production, a blade starts from plate or bar and reaches its profile mainly by cutting, grinding and machining material away. In forging, a billet or thicker piece of steel is first deformed toward the required distribution of material and is then still cut, ground, heat-treated and finished. Forging can be especially useful when the design needs a thick integral bolster, a local change in thickness, a tapered section or another shape that would otherwise require removing a large amount of material from uniform stock. Forging can also change the internal condition of steel during manufacture. Hot working can break down the cast structure of an ingot, redistribute segregated constituents and, under suitable conditions, help refine the structure before later processing. These effects matter in steelmaking, but they should not be turned into the claim that every forged kitchen knife is metallurgically superior. Modern blade steel normally reaches the knife maker after substantial industrial processing such as forging and rolling has already occurred at the steel mill. A knife cut from high-quality rolled plate is therefore not made from raw, untouched metal. The finished knife still depends on the steel composition, the quality of the starting stock, temperature control during forging, heat treatment, grinding, edge geometry and final workmanship. Poor forging or overheating can damage steel just as poor heat treatment can. An excellent stock-removal knife can outperform a poorly forged one, and a carefully forged knife can use its manufacturing route to create shapes or material distribution that would be inefficient by stock removal. This also explains why visible hammer marks are not proof of forging quality. A forged blade can be ground and polished completely smooth, while a textured surface can be deliberately created or retained for appearance. The useful question is therefore not simply **“Is it forged?”** but **“What did forging contribute to this design, and how well were the steel, heat treatment and geometry executed afterwards?”** Forging and tang construction answer different questions. Forging describes **how steel is shaped during manufacture**; full, hidden, through and partial tang describe **how the blade continues into the handle**. Keeping those ideas separate makes the next handle construction easier to understand. ## What this book calls an “Asian handle” In this book, **Asian handle** means the traditional hidden-tang construction commonly paired with an **octagonal**, and sometimes oval, handle. The narrower tang disappears inside the handle instead of remaining visible between side scales. A **collar** reinforces the front of the handle, while some modern constructions also use an internal **dowel insert** to guide and receive the tang. The term is intentionally narrow. It does **not** mean that all knives made in Asia use this construction; many use Western full-tang, molded or other systems. Here, **Asian handle** means the octagonal-or-oval hidden-tang construction with the front collar described above. A **collar** is different from a Western bolster. Both sit near the blade-handle junction, but the collar reinforces the front of the handle, while the bolster is a metal component at the blade-handle transition. The dowel insert shown in the exploded Xinzuo construction is one assembly method; it is not a defining feature of every Asian handle. ## Geometry and material: what anatomy alone cannot tell you Anatomy tells us **where** a feature is; it does not by itself tell us how that feature will behave. A thin blade bends more easily than a thick one because of geometry, while the steel and heat treatment determine how much bending, impact or twisting the blade can tolerate without permanent damage or fracture. This distinction matters when comparing a flexible fillet knife, a rigid precision slicer and a bone chopper. Their visible dimensions, steel and heat treatment are designed together for different loads. Do not test a hard precision knife by deliberately bending it: flexibility is not a quality test, and a thin hard blade may chip, crack or break when forced sideways. The later steel chapters explain hardness, toughness, edge retention and microstructure in detail. For now, keep one principle: **geometry determines the load placed on the material; material and heat treatment determine how the knife responds to that load.** ## Understanding blade-face features Do not treat every visible surface feature as the same kind of treatment. **First: what is the topography?** Hollows, channels and hammered depressions change the physical shape of the blade face. By interrupting broad contact, they may reduce suction or sticking with some moist or starchy foods. Depth, position and spacing matter more than the decorative name. A chef's knife with hollows remains a chef's knife because its working profile has not changed category. **Second: what texture did finishing leave?** Satin grinding leaves directional lines; polishing reduces surface roughness and mirror polishing reduces it further. Texture affects drag, scratch visibility and cleaning, but it does not create sharpness at the apex. **Third: did the surface reveal or retain a structure?** Etching can expose contrast between Damascus layers. Hand forging can leave irregular scale or texture when the face is not ground completely smooth. A retained forged surface and deliberate hammering may look related, but they come from different processes and should be described separately. Food release depends on topography, blade geometry, finish, food and movement together. No pattern or polish can replace suitable thickness and cross-section. With the parts and construction terms established, the next chapter examines **how the blade narrows toward the cutting edge**. Understanding bevel geometry first makes the later comparison of complete knife shapes much easier.

units.source: ## Blade terminology
units.masked_source: ## Blade terminology

units.source: The **tip** is the front of the blade. Its shape affects how easily the knife enters small spaces, scores a surface or makes fine directional corrections. The **spine** is the upper, normally unsharpened side. Its thickness and taper toward the tip affect stiffness, balance and how easily the blade passes through food.
units.masked_source: The **tip** is the front of the blade. Its shape affects how easily the knife enters small spaces, scores a surface or makes fine directional corrections. The **spine** is the upper, normally unsharpened side. Its thickness and taper toward the tip affect stiffness, balance and how easily the blade passes through food.

units.source: The broad side is the **blade face**. It is not always flat: convexity, hollows, cladding transitions and other shaping can change how food moves against it. The **surface finish** is the final texture or appearance on that face, such as satin, polished, mirror-polished, brushed, etched or hammered. Finish and geometry are different: two blades can look similar while having very different thickness and cross-section.

units.source: The **cutting edge** or **edge** is the sharpened line that enters the food. Above it, the **bevel** narrows the blade toward the apex. Some knives have a clearly visible primary bevel; on others the transition is subtle. The **heel** is the rear of the cutting edge, closest to the handle. Depending on the design, a short unsharpened area or relief may separate it from the bolster or handle.

units.source: ## Handle, bolster and tang
units.masked_source: ## Handle, bolster and tang

units.source: The **handle** is the part held by the user, but its construction varies. On a Western **full-tang** knife, the tang runs through almost the full length and outline of the handle. **Scales** cover its sides and are usually secured with adhesive and **rivets or pins**. The exposed steel can add mass and affect balance.

On a Western **full-tang** knife, the tang runs through almost the full length and outline of the handle. **Scales** cover its sides and are usually secured with adhesive and **rivets or pins**. The exposed steel can add mass and affect balance.

units.source: **Full tang is only one valid tang construction.** A **hidden tang** is narrower than the handle and enclosed inside it. Some hidden tangs extend all the way to the butt and are mechanically secured there; this is a **through tang**, a separate construction term and not another name for a full tang. A **partial or stub tang** ends before the butt. Molded handles can encapsulate the tang so no scales or rivets are visible. These constructions should not be treated as a simple quality hierarchy: durability depends on tang dimensions, materials, fit, fastening, intended use and expected loads.

units.source: With the tang identified, the next part to distinguish is the **blade-to-handle transition**. A **bolster** is the reinforced metal transition found on many Western kitchen knives. It may be integral with the blade or manufactured as a separate component. It can strengthen the transition, create a comfortable finger contact point, protect the front of the handle and add mass near the hand. Some bolsters extend to the heel; others leave the edge open for easier sharpening. A bolster is not necessarily a **guard**. A guard is specifically designed to stop the hand sliding toward the edge, and many kitchen knives have no separate guard.

Some bolsters extend to the heel; others leave the edge open for easier sharpening. A bolster is not necessarily a **guard**. units.source: On many high-quality production knives, a separate bolster is joined to the blade-and-tang assembly by **welding** and is then ground and finished as part of the complete knife. The presence of a welded joint is not, by itself, a sign of lower quality. In hurried or poorly controlled manufacture, inaccurate fit or an inadequate joint can make this transition a structurally sensitive point. When the parts fit correctly and the joint, heat control and finishing are properly executed, the bolster can instead stiffen and reinforce the blade-to-handle transition and help distribute loads through that area.

units.source: A common question is why the bolster is not simply made from the same high-performance steel as the blade. The first reason is functional: the bolster does not form the cutting edge, so using an expensive specialist blade steel there usually adds material cost without improving cutting performance. A separate component allows each material to be chosen for the work it actually performs: the blade steel for edge behaviour and the bolster material for structure, corrosion resistance, finish, manufacturability and reliable joining.

units.source: There is also an important manufacturing reason. If an integral bolster is produced by **machining from uniform plate or bar stock**, the starting material has to be at least as thick as the bolster even though the blade and much of the tang are far thinner. A large proportion of that expensive steel must then be removed to create the final blade geometry. This wastes both premium material and machining time. Forging can create an integral bolster by a different route and reduces the need to machine the whole knife from bolster-thickness stock, so the exact economics depend on the manufacturing process. In production based on plate or bar, however, making the bolster separately is often the more rational solution: expensive blade steel is concentrated where its properties matter instead of being consumed simply to create a thick non-cutting section.

units.source: ### What forging actually means
units.masked_source: ### What forging actually means

units.source: That manufacturing comparison raises a term that is often mistaken for a quality label. **Forging is a manufacturing process, not a quality grade.** The steel remains solid and is reshaped by compressive force so that material moves from one part of the workpiece to another. Knife forging is usually done hot because heated steel requires less force to deform. A hand hammer is only one way to supply that force: power hammers, mechanical or hydraulic presses and industrial dies can all forge steel. A knife can therefore be genuinely forged without being handmade, and a hand-forged knife is not automatically a better knife.

A hand hammer is only one way to supply that force: power hammers, mechanical or hydraulic presses and industrial dies can all forge steel. A knife can therefore be genuinely forged without being handmade, and a hand-forged knife is not automatically a better knife.

units.source: The practical contrast is with **stock removal**. In stock-removal production, a blade starts from plate or bar and reaches its profile mainly by cutting, grinding and machining material away. In forging, a billet or thicker piece of steel is first deformed toward the required distribution of material and is then still cut, ground, heat-treated and finished. Forging can be especially useful when the design needs a thick integral bolster, a local change in thickness, a tapered section or another shape that would otherwise require removing a large amount of material from uniform stock.

Hot working can break down the cast structure of an ingot, redistribute segregated constituents and, under suitable conditions, help refine the structure before later processing. These effects matter in steelmaking, but they should not be turned into the claim that every forged kitchen knife is metallurgically superior. Modern blade steel normally reaches the knife maker after substantial industrial processing such as forging and rolling has already occurred at the steel mill. A knife cut from high-quality rolled plate is therefore not made from raw, untouched metal.

pages.page_context:
# The Five Dimensions of Knife Steel

Begin with the work the edge must perform. A long slicing session, repeated contact with acidic food and occasional work near joints place different demands on steel. HRC, edge retention and alloy price describe only parts of that problem.

One steel may hold an edge for a long time but require demanding abrasives. Another may sharpen easily but need more frequent maintenance. A highly corrosion-resistant steel may suit a busy kitchen, while a reactive carbon steel may suit someone who values sharpening response and is willing to clean and dry the blade immediately.

The useful question is:

> Which balance of qualities best suits this knife, this task and this user?

Five dimensions provide a practical framework: **hardness, sharpening response, corrosion resistance, toughness and microstructural fineness**. *Microstructure* means the microscopic internal structure of the steel: its tiny crystals, phases and hard particles. The later metallurgy chapters explain these parts in more detail.

## 1. Hardness: resistance to permanent deformation

Hardness is resistance to indentation and permanent deformation. Kitchen-knife hardness is commonly reported on the Rockwell C scale, abbreviated **HRC**.

HRC does not measure sharpness, toughness or overall cutting performance. A knife is sharp because its edge is geometrically fine and clean. Hardness helps determine how that geometry changes during use.

A harder apex generally resists rolling and plastic deformation better. Hardness also contributes to abrasive wear resistance. With broadly similar steel composition and microstructure, the harder sample usually resists wear more strongly.

Steel can also contain **carbides: microscopic hard crystals formed when carbon combines with iron or certain alloying elements**. Carbide type, amount, size and distribution can change wear resistance greatly. Vanadium- or niobium-rich carbides, for example, are much harder than the surrounding steel matrix.

The **matrix** is the continuous part of the steel that surrounds these particles. Its own hardness matters too. Two steels at the same HRC can therefore behave differently because their matrices and carbide populations are different.

The practical rule is simple: **do not rank unrelated steels by HRC alone**. Evaluate hardness together with heat treatment, microstructure, edge angle, thickness behind the edge and intended use.

Higher hardness can also reduce tolerance for misuse. A very hard, thin edge may remain extremely stable in correct cutting yet tolerate twisting, levering or impact poorly. Hardness works best when the steel's toughness and blade geometry suit the intended task.

## 2. Sharpening response: more than “soft equals easy”

Sharpening response describes how readily and predictably an abrasive can restore the apex. Hardness is only part of the picture.

A harder matrix resists abrasion more strongly, but carbides can matter even more. Large volumes of very hard carbides slow material removal and may need efficient ceramic or diamond abrasives. Burr behaviour matters too. One steel may form a small, crisp burr that releases cleanly; another may form a persistent wire edge that takes more work to remove.

The shortcut **“softer steel is easier to sharpen” is unreliable**. A moderately soft stainless steel may be forgiving in use without giving clear feedback on a water stone. A well heat-treated high-carbon steel can have much higher HRC yet abrade quickly, give clear feedback and deburr cleanly.

DIN 1.4116 shows the difference well. Kitchen knives often use it at moderate hardness, which can make them forgiving in everyday use. That does not make the steel inherently easy to sharpen. Depending on heat treatment, geometry and abrasive, it can develop a tenacious burr and feel less clean on the stone than a fine, simple carbon steel. **Blue Steel No. 2 (Aogami #2) can respond very readily to suitable water stones even though it is commonly used at much higher hardness.**

Keep two ideas separate:

- **forgiving use**: how readily the edge tolerates deformation or ordinary mistakes;
- **sharpening response**: how efficiently the steel abrades, reaches the apex and deburrs.

They affect each other, but they are not the same property.

## 3. Corrosion resistance: what “stainless” means

Corrosion resistance is a blade's ability to resist moisture, oxygen, salt, acids and other substances encountered in use.

The widely used compositional threshold for stainless steel is **at least 10.5% chromium by mass**. This classifies the steel; it does not mean every steel above the threshold resists corrosion equally well.

Chromium works mainly through **passivation**. This means that enough chromium at the surface forms an extremely thin protective oxide layer that slows further corrosion. If scratched, the film can form again when suitable conditions return.

The key word is *available*. Chromium dissolved in the matrix can support passivation; chromium tied up in carbides is less available for that job. Carbon content, heat treatment, molybdenum, nitrogen, surface finish and the working environment all affect the result.

Stainless steel is corrosion-resistant, not stain-proof. Salt, chlorides, acidic residue and prolonged wet storage can still stain or pit a stainless blade. Reactive carbon steels need faster care and may develop a dark patina, which is different from active orange rust.

## 4. Toughness: resistance to fracture

**Toughness** is the ability to absorb stress and energy without fracturing. At the edge, low toughness may appear as chipping. At a larger scale it can lead to cracking or breakage under impact, twisting or strong lateral loads.

Toughness is narrower than the everyday idea of *robustness*. A finished knife also gains or loses robustness through thickness, edge angle, blade shape and the amount of material supporting the edge.

The same steel can feel delicate in an extremely thin precision slicer and much more tolerant in a thicker working geometry. Even a very tough steel cannot make an ultrathin edge immune to lateral abuse.

The task determines the useful compromise. A sashimi slicer benefits from refinement and low cutting resistance; a bone chopper needs much more support behind the edge.

## 5. Microstructural fineness: what supports the apex

Steel looks uniform to the eye, but under a microscope it is made from many tiny crystal **grains** and can contain different phases and carbide crystals. Their size, amount and distribution affect wear resistance, toughness and how finely the edge can be refined.

A finer, more uniform microstructure generally supports a very fine, continuous apex more easily. This does not mean the edge radius must match the diameter of the largest carbide. The mechanism is more complex. The useful point is that very large hard particles can make an extremely smooth, continuous edge harder to create and stabilize.

Large or abundant hard carbides can still be useful. They can increase wear resistance and preserve an aggressive, toothy slicing character for a long time. The trade-off is usually slower sharpening, while high carbide size or volume can reduce toughness and the potential for an ultra-refined apex.

The term **grain size** is sometimes used loosely for all of this, but grain size and carbide size are different. This guide uses *microstructural fineness* as the broader teaching term. The later metallurgy chapters explain grains, matrix, phases and the main carbide families in more detail.

## The five dimensions interact

The five dimensions are not independent properties that can all be maximized at the same time.

- Higher hardness can improve resistance to rolling and wear while reducing tolerance for some forms of misuse.
- More hard carbides can improve abrasive wear resistance while slowing sharpening and often reducing toughness.
- Strong corrosion resistance depends on alloy balance and chromium available for passivation, not simply on nominal chromium content.
- Very thin geometry can transform cutting performance while demanding more from the steel and the user.
- A steel can sharpen easily and still hold an edge well, or have moderate hardness and still resist sharpening.

These trade-offs are why different steels and heat treatments exist.

## Applying the five dimensions to the Xinzuo range

Xinzuo uses the five dimensions as different design directions rather than trying to make one steel serve every knife. The breadth of the range is deliberate: **different steels are selected or developed because different users and cutting tasks need different balances**.

The [Xinzuo Blade Steels](../02-steels-and-metallurgy/xinzuo-blade-steels.md) chapter shows this strategy in practice. ZDP-189 emphasizes very high hardness and wear resistance; SRS13 and M390 pursue different premium powder-steel balances; proprietary 14Cr14MoVNb combines high hardness and retention with Xinzuo's direct involvement in alloy development; 10Cr15CoMoV occupies a broad all-round position with particularly strong corrosion stability; Blue Steel No. 2 exchanges stainless convenience for responsive carbon-steel behaviour; and DIN 1.4116 serves the more forgiving, moderate-hardness end of the range.

The material strategy is matched by process control. Selected series use **vacuum heat treatment and deep-freeze processing** to obtain more of the performance available from demanding steels, while controlled grinding and sharpening preserve that result through final production. Xinzuo therefore works on both sides of the equation: choosing or developing the alloy balance and then controlling how that material becomes a finished edge.

A home cook may value corrosion resistance and tolerance of ordinary use. A professional making precise fish or vegetable cuts may accept more demanding care for greater hardness, fine geometry and sharpening response. A butcher working around joints may put toughness and blade support ahead of extreme refinement.

These priorities serve different work. Xinzuo addresses them through multiple material and design strategies, allowing steel, geometry and balance to be matched to the task and user rather than defining one configuration as universally premium.

The central lesson is more useful than “higher is better”:

> **A steel grade describes potential. Heat treatment develops the microstructure, geometry determines how the edge meets food, and the user's technique determines which trade-offs matter in practice.**
